entry.evidence: Therefore, understanding year-round discharge responses, in particular the sensitivity of stream discharge to changes in yearly snowfall fractions, is warranted

sequences.source_document: g22_W4281628857.xml.txt (publisher XML text of the published paper)

steps.action: The authors pose three research questions on how SWI varies between wet, dry, rainy and snowy years, how discharge responds to it, and whether discharge tracks snowfall fraction.
steps.quote: Are variations in stream discharge related to variations in yearly snowfall fractions?

steps.action: The authors take from the literature the expectation that a lower snowfall fraction lowers stream discharge.
steps.quote: a decrease in the fraction of precipitation falling as snow (snowfall fraction hereinafter) is expected to decrease stream discharge

steps.action: The authors use hourly weather, snow depth and weir discharge records from 11 Johnston Draw stations, published earlier by co-author Godsey and colleagues.
steps.quote: We used hourly hydrometeorological data recorded at 11 weather stations throughout the catchment

steps.action: The authors difference a snow-on lidar flight (18 March 2009) from a snow-off flight (2007) to map snow depth at 1 m, with an uncertainty of about 14 cm.
steps.quote: a 1 m resolution snow depth product was calculated as the difference between a snow-off lidar flight

steps.action: The authors check the lidar snow depths against the station snow depths and find a consistent offset with a strong linear relation (r2 = 0.88, Fig. S1).
steps.quote: a strong linear relation between the two individual sets of snow depth measurements

steps.action: The authors build a 3 m snow-covered-area product from 41 PlanetScope images, using principal component analysis and a manually trained maximum likelihood classification that includes a shaded-snow class.
steps.quote: We used the Maximum Likelihood Classification tool in ArcMap (Esri Inc., 2020) to identify the SCA

steps.action: The authors read snowpack melt-out dates for 2016-2019 off the imagery by eye, with an error of about 2 days.
steps.quote: We also used the surface reflectance imagery to determine the melt-out date of the snowpack

steps.action: The authors force AWSM (SMRF distribution plus the iSnobal energy-balance model) with the station data at 10 m resolution to estimate precipitation phase, snowpack and SWI, excluding the undercatching jd124 gauge.
steps.quote: We used the Automated Water Supply Model (AWSM; Havens et al., 2020) to obtain spatially continuous estimates of the distribution and phase of precipitation

steps.action: From 11 years of record the authors select four contrasting water years (rainy 2005, snowy 2010, wet 2011, dry 2014), plus 2009 for its lidar survey.
steps.quote: we chose 2005, 2010, 2011, and 2014 because they are hydroclimatically different

steps.action: The authors rescale snowfall in every year with the 2009 lidar snow depth pattern (the Vögeli et al. 2016 approach, as extended by Trujillo et al. 2019) to represent wind redistribution.
steps.quote: we use the precipitation rescaling approach proposed by Vögeli et al. (2016)

steps.action: The authors check the premise that the snow distribution is consistent between years by comparing the 2009 lidar snow depths with the 2019 satellite snow cover.
steps.quote: verification of the interannual consistency in the snow distribution in this catchment by comparing the lidar snow depth and the satellite imagery

steps.action: The authors design the comparison of precipitation and SWI metrics (seasonal sums, flashiness index, melt rate, snow-cover duration) with annual discharge and stream dry-out date, with no lag.
steps.quote: The phase and magnitude of precipitation and the magnitude and temporal distribution of SWI were compared to annual discharge and the stream dry-out date

steps.action: The authors describe the lidar snow depth distribution: north-south aspect contrasts, wind scour, and drifts up to 5.3 m deep.
steps.quote: Large snowdrifts formed in some western parts of the watershed, up to a maximum depth of 5.3 m

steps.action: The authors compare simulated snow depth with lidar (r2 = 0.88), and simulated 2009 snow cover with 2019 satellite snow cover; the model underestimates snow duration in the scour zone.
steps.quote: Simulated snow depths on the day of the lidar survey agreed well with the lidar snow depth

steps.action: The authors score simulated snow depths against station records with NSE, normalized NSE and RMSE for all five years and report low NSE at some sites in 2011.
steps.quote: the normalized snow depths were largely acceptable (35 out of 40 year–location combinations had a NSE norm value above 0.5

steps.action: The authors map annual SWI for the four years and find the same spatial pattern each year: highest in the drifts, higher on north-facing and northeast-facing slopes.
steps.quote: The spatial pattern of SWI was similar for all years, with the highest SWI occurring in the snowdrifts

steps.action: The authors estimate the weekly and seasonal timing of SWI and its rain and snowmelt parts, and find steadier inputs in snowy 2010.
steps.quote: Overall, variations in weekly and daily SWI rates were lower in snowy 2010 (CV daily SWI of 1.71) than in all other years

steps.action: The authors compare SWI with discharge through the year and find little response early in the water year and strong response to high-rate events such as rain on snow.
steps.quote: Streamflow was least responsive to SWI at the beginning of each water year (Fig. 5).

steps.action: The authors relate annual discharge to snowfall fraction (no relation) and, adding unsimulated years, to precipitation at jd125 (r2 = 0.83).
steps.quote: there was no relation between annual discharge and the annual snowfall fraction (Fig. 6c)

steps.action: The authors test for a memory effect by adding the previous year's precipitation; the correlation weakens, so they set storage memory aside.
steps.quote: This indicates that any memory effect is likely to be small in this catchment.

steps.action: The authors screen Pearson correlations (alpha = 0.1) of annual discharge and dry-out date against precipitation, SWI and snowpack metrics over 5 to 11 years.
steps.quote: No significant correlation was found between the annual, winter, and spring snowfall fraction and annual discharge and the stream dry-out date (Fig. 7).

steps.action: The authors keep the claim of a spatially consistent SWI pattern while noting that the rescaling builds it in, and they rest it on the independent satellite agreement.
steps.quote: In our modeling routine, the spatial consistency between years is pre-determined by the snowfall rescaling

steps.action: The authors set the drift share of SWE and SWI against earlier Reynolds Mountain East studies.
steps.quote: Previous work in the seasonally snow-covered Reynolds Mountain East catchment showed that snowdrifts indeed hold a large fraction of total catchment snow water equivalent

steps.action: The authors relate stream dry-out date to snowpack melt-out date over 9 years (r2 = 0.74, Fig. 6b) and infer that the drifts sustain streamflow.
steps.quote: the stream dry-out date was positively correlated with the drift melt-out date (Fig. 6b)

steps.action: The authors propose, after the fact, that steadier snowmelt inputs and deeper flow paths explain why 2010 had twice the discharge of 2005 and why flow lasts after melt-out.
steps.quote: The steadier water inputs in the snowmelt period might explain why annual discharge in snowy 2010 was double that of rainy 2005

steps.action: The authors relate summer and winter runoff efficiency to air temperature (Figs. S10, S11).
steps.quote: Air temperature also has a small effect on the runoff efficiency, particularly in the summer season.

steps.action: The authors reject their own hypothesis, and the Berghuijs et al. (2014) expectation, that snowfall fraction controls discharge and stream cessation at this site.
steps.quote: [...] annual discharge nor the stream dry-out date were correlated with snowfall fraction (Figs. 6, 7)

steps.action: The authors bound the range of the finding: the timing of SWI may matter less in more humid or larger catchments.
steps.quote: The temporal distribution of SWI might be less important for predicting stream discharge and cessation in more humid catchments

steps.action: The authors compare with Bilish et al. (2020) in the Australian Alps and with Dry Creek observations, which also show no link between snowfall fraction and streamflow in small catchments.
steps.quote: Bilish et al. (2020) similarly found that streamflow was not correlated with the snowfall fraction

steps.action: The authors explain the poor 2011 snow depth fits with an auxiliary (denser snow and weaker wind, so less redistribution than in 2009) rather than rejecting the model.
steps.quote: To investigate why simulations of snow depths were poor for some stations and years

steps.action: The authors add three further auxiliary reasons for the misfits (precipitation phase errors, grid versus point scale, evaluation on depth rather than SWE) and keep the SWI result.
steps.quote: we suggest three additional reasons for the differences between simulated and observed snow depths

steps.action: The authors conclude that discharge is insensitive to snowfall fraction, depends on total and spring precipitation, and that stream cessation tracks snowdrift persistence.
steps.quote: Over the 2004–2014 data record, annual discharge was insensitive to snowfall fraction and depended more on total and spring precipitation.

end.claim: In a small semiarid rain–snow transition catchment over 2004-2014, annual discharge and stream dry-out date did not correlate with snowfall fraction but with total and spring precipitation, and dry-out date also with snowdrift melt-out date.

decisive_move.sentence: The correlation screen of discharge and dry-out date against snowfall-fraction, precipitation and SWI metrics across the recorded years produces the headline relations; without it there is no claim about snowfall-fraction sensitivity.

gates.evidence: The years were chosen for contrasting snowfall fraction and precipitation (§3.3 ¶2), so the question shaped the selection; but 'our hypothesis' is named only in the Discussion (§5.2 ¶2). The snowfall-fraction hypothesis could fail and did, but with n = 5-11 years and many correlations at alpha = 0.1 the test is weak (inference). Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Airborne lidar differencing for snow depth
PlanetScope 3 m four-band surface reflectance imagery
Principal component analysis to condense spectral bands

novelty_claims.quote: [...] in snowfall fractions in the rain–snow transition zone contrasts [...] studies on snow-related processes that focus on seasonally snow-covered catchments
here we focus on hourly responses at a fine spatial resolution
Our method differs from other satellite-derived snow products that combine both visible and infrared light, but it yielded a higher-resolution data product

limits: No review file or open discussion was supplied, so no review sequence is coded, although the paper went through HESSD discussion. Sub-claims: the spatial SWI pattern (drifts up to 6-7 times the catchment average) is estimate_with_resolution at best; SWI itself is never validated against data, only snow depth and snow cover, and no uncertainty is given for SWI. Its consistency between years is built in by the 2009-lidar snowfall rescaling (§5.1 ¶1). The authors support it with the independent satellite agreement, which compares 2009 against 2019 only. The dry-out/melt-out relation is regularity_in_range on n = 9, and the drift mechanism is untested because neither subsurface flow nor streamflow generation was measured or simulated (§5.1 ¶2). The post hoc explanations (steadier snowmelt inputs, deeper flow paths) are best_explanation without a test. Internal inconsistencies: the abstract says 'up to 6 times' and §5.1 'up to 7 times'; §5.1 gives 2005 SWIavg as 573 mm while Table 1 gives 557; §4.4 attributes 553 and 557 mm to 2005 and 2010 the other way round from Table 1. The correlation screen tests many metrics at alpha = 0.1 without correction for multiple comparisons (inference). The authors' hypothesis is first named in the Discussion, so it is unclear when it was formed (inference).

disagreements.support: Over 11 years at Johnston Draw neither annual discharge nor dry-out date correlated with snowfall fraction; the authors suggest the earlier result may hold for larger or more humid catchments.
disagreements.quote: In contrast with our hypothesis and what has been suggested in the literature

disagreements.target: Use of SWE as the summarizing variable for winter precipitation in discharge comparisons
disagreements.support: The authors argue that SWI is more directly tied to the timing and amount of water resources, and they model it.
disagreements.quote: while SWE is frequently used as a summarizing variable for winter precipitation when comparing precipitation to stream discharge, SWI is [...]
